titre: No Parliament Can Bind Its Successor
accroche: In 1885, the jurist Albert Venn Dicey formulates the sovereignty of the British Parliament: no law can prevent the next one from undoing it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Oxford, 1885. Albert Venn Dicey, a professor of law and, since 1882, holder of the Vinerian chair, publishes the *Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution*, in which he tries to put into a formula what English constitutional practice had until then left unformulated. He writes there that the British Parliament “has the right to make or unmake any law whatever; and further, that no person or body is recognised by the law of England as having a right to override or set aside the legislation of Parliament.”

## A sovereignty with no higher text

The formula answers a precise question: what, in English law, prevents one statute from undoing another? In a written constitution like that of the United States or France, an ordinary law contrary to the Constitution can be annulled by a judge, and the Constitution itself can be amended only under strengthened conditions (a qualified majority, a referendum, the agreement of both chambers). The United Kingdom has no text of that rank: no statute there is constitutionally superior to another, and Parliament can pass, amend, or repeal any of them by simple majority, including those that touch the very organization of the state.

The consequence, which Dicey states as self-evident, is that a Parliament cannot commit itself for the future. A law that claimed to forbid its own future repeal, or to impose on its successors a heavier procedure to undo it, would remain in English law a law like any other: the next Parliament could repeal it by simple majority, exactly as it repeals any other text. No law can therefore, in theory, bind the one that comes after it.

## A doctrine tested for nearly fifty years

The principle faced its first real stress test with the United Kingdom's entry into the European Economic Community through the European Communities Act of 1972: that law gave Community law a primacy that British judges would recognize, in practice, even over later statutes contradicting it. This is, on its face, a breach of the very principle that nothing can bind a future Parliament. Jurists and judges debated for nearly fifty years whether that primacy was a real exception to parliamentary sovereignty or merely an ordinary statute, repealable like any other. The United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union, in 2020, made the debate largely theoretical without ever settling it in law.

carte.punch: A law that forbade its own repeal would remain, in English law, a law like any other.
carte.idee: In 1885, the jurist Albert Venn Dicey formulates the sovereignty of the British Parliament: it can make or unmake any law, and no law can bind the one that comes after it, not even a law that claimed to protect itself.

quiz.question: According to the doctrine formulated by Dicey, what would happen if the British Parliament passed a law forbidding its own future repeal?
choix: It would bind all later Parliaments, like a higher constitutional norm
Only a supreme court could then repeal it, and no longer Parliament itself
The next Parliament could repeal it by simple majority, like any other law
It could be repealed only by the unanimity of both houses of Parliament
quiz.explication: For Dicey, no law is hierarchically superior to another in English law: a law that forbade its own repeal would remain, like the others, within reach of a later Parliament voting by simple majority. That is the very meaning of parliamentary sovereignty.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which chair does Dicey hold at Oxford when he publishes his book in 1885?
choix: The Vinerian chair, which he has held since 1882
The Regius chair of civil law
The chair of philosophy of law, created especially for him
None: he teaches as a lecturer without a chair
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Dicey has held the Vinerian chair at Oxford since 1882 when he publishes his book in 1885.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why can an ordinary law contrary to the Constitution be annulled by a judge in the United States or France, but not in the United Kingdom?
choix: Because British judges have no right to rule on statutes
Because the United Kingdom has no text constitutionally superior to other laws
Because the British Parliament never passed a written constitution before the twentieth century
Because British courts did not yet exist in 1885
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text contrasts a written constitution, where a contrary law can be annulled by a judge, with the absence in the United Kingdom of any constitutionally superior text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what does the European Communities Act of 1972 change in practice?
choix: It writes parliamentary sovereignty into a text for the first time
It transfers to the European Parliament the power to repeal British laws
It gives Community law a primacy that British judges would recognize even over later statutes
It definitively ends, in law, the debate over parliamentary sovereignty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: That law gives Community law a primacy that judges would recognize in practice even against later statutes contradicting it.
